questions.q: For $f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2$, what are $\nabla f$ and $|\nabla f|$ at $(3, 4)$?
questions.explain: $\nabla f = [2x, 2y] = [6, 8]$ and $|\nabla f| = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$. Adding components ($14$) is not a vector length.

questions.q: Which direction does $\nabla f$ point, and which direction does gradient descent move?
options: $\nabla f$ points steepest uphill; descent follows $-\nabla f$
$\nabla f$ points steepest downhill; descent follows $+\nabla f$
$\nabla f$ points along the contour lines; descent follows them too
$\nabla f$ always points toward the origin
questions.explain: The gradient is the direction of steepest ascent. Training wants lower loss, so it steps along $-\nabla L$.

questions.q: On the Saddle $f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2$, the gradient at $(0, 0)$ is $[0, 0]$. What does that tell you?
options: The surface is flat there, but it is neither a min nor a max — it is a saddle point
questions.explain: $\nabla f = [2x, -2y] = [0, 0]$, yet $f$ rises along $x$ and falls along $y$. A zero gradient does not guarantee a minimum or maximum.

questions.q: Why is $\nabla f$ described as a vector rather than a number?
options: Because it lists the function values at several points
Because it is always a unit vector
Because it is the sum of the partial derivatives
Because it has both a direction (steepest uphill) and a magnitude (how steep)
questions.explain: $\nabla f = \left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\right]$ stacks the partials; its direction is steepest ascent and its length $|\nabla f|$ is the steepness. It is not normalized to length 1.
